title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student’s token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has been driven by complementary progress in model architectures ( He et al., 2016 ; Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Yu et al., 2026a ) , data scale and quality ( Yuan et al., 2023 ; Rao et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026b ) , and training paradigms ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . Current research frontiers span theoretical explorations of learning dynamics and generalization ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) , generation across various modalities ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2026 ) , tool-augmented reasoning ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and interdisciplinary applications ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . Within this broad landscape, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a central paradigm for exploring complex reasoning and knowledge transfer. A key challenge is how to enable smaller student models to efficiently inherit the capabilities of stronger teachers. Figure 1: Overview of CoRD . (i) Left (OPD’s blind spot): On-policy distillation trains only on student rollouts. Teacher-preferred reasoning paths that the student rarely or never visits therefore receive little or no supervision. (ii) Right (our coupled sampler): CoRD keeps the same training loss and budget, but changes the rollout sampler. By coupling the student with a teacher-leaning target q α q_{\alpha} , it preserves agreeing tokens and replaces disagreements with underweighted target tokens. This maximal coupling steers rollouts into teacher-preferred states missed by OPD with the minimum possible intervention rate, minimally perturbing the student’s original trajectory. Among knowledge distillation methods, on-policy distillation (OPD) has become a commonly used approach to this challenge Agarwal et al. (2024) ; Gu et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2024) . The student generates its own rollouts and is trained to match the teacher’s full next-token distribution at every state it visits, usually by minimizing the reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence. Training on self-generated text removes the mismatch between teacher-forced training and free-running generation Bengio et al. (2015) ; Ranzato et al. (2016) ; Ross et al. (2011) , and the teacher’s dense, token-level signal replaces the single final reward of reinforcement learning. The same design also fixes where the supervision lands. Because states are drawn from the student, the teacher only ever comments on states the student already reaches. States the teacher would enter, such as the first step of a solution path the student considers unlikely, are sampled only as often as the student itself picks them, and corrected only that often. We measure this blind spot on frozen sets of states. Before training, the student is 1.5 to 2.4 times further from the teacher on states reached by the teacher’s distribution than on states it reaches itself, across the four students analyzed in Section 5 . On-policy training closes this gap only slowly: after 40 steps at 4B, OPD has removed 15.0% of the divergence on teacher-reached states, where the sampler we introduce removes 21.7%. Reaching those states requires steering the rollout toward the teacher while leaving it the student’s own text wherever the two agree. Speculative decoding already contains the right tool Leviathan et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2023) . Its rejection sampler, usually seen as an accelerator, realizes the maximal coupling of two token distributions Lindvall (1992) : a draft token is kept where the distributions agree and replaced by a draw from their difference where they do not. When used instead as a training sampler, this rule intervenes only where the student and the target disagree, and exactly as often as they disagree. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), illustrated in Figure 1 , which changes the rollout sampler of OPD and nothing else. At each position the student proposes a token, and the coupling with a tempered target q α ∝ p S 1 − α ​ p T α q_{\alpha}\propto p_{\mathrm{S}}^{1-\alpha}p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\alpha} either keeps it or substitutes a token from the residual mass that the student underweights. Every emitted token is an exact draw from q α q_{\alpha} , the probability of an intervention equals the total-variation distance between p S p_{\mathrm{S}} and q α q_{\alpha} , and α = 0 \alpha=0 recovers OPD bit for bit. The loss, the teacher, and the number of training steps stay as they are; only the distribution of training states moves toward the teacher. That shift is the source of the gain. The coupling is how CoRD reaches the shifted states while rewriting as little of the student’s own text as any exact sampler of q α q_{\alpha} can, and it splits every draw into an acceptance decision and a replacement direction, which Section 5 tests separately. The shift pays off on public benchmarks. Across six base students from two model families, CoRD improves average pass@1 and pass@8 over OPD on MATH500, AIME24, AIME25, AMC23 and GSM8K for every student in Table 1 ; on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, SKD’s published replacement rule Xu et al. (2025) , with the same loss and budget, lands between OPD and CoRD , and OPD trained for twice as many steps does not catch up. The difficulty breakdown shows that each student’s largest pass@16 gain is on problems it rarely or never solved before training, although the aggregate pass@16 gain is not positive for every student. Substitution rules that intervene at least as often but draw the replacement from elsewhere, namely a uniform token, a token from the student’s average distribution, or a teacher sample at randomly chosen positions, stay at or near OPD and far below CoRD , which ties the gain to where the rollouts are steered rather than to the act of intervening. Our contributions are as follows: • We measure the blind spot of on-policy distillation on frozen sets of teacher-reached states, where the student starts 1.5 to 2.4 times further from the teacher than on its own states, and show that OPD leaves most of it in place. • We propose CoRD , which trains on rollouts from a teacher-leaning target and realizes them with the speculative-decoding rejection sampler: exact draws from the target with the fewest possible replacements (the total-variation distance), and OPD as the special case α = 0 \alpha=0 . • We show gains in average pass@1 and pass@8 over OPD for all six base students on five public math benchmarks, and study teacher-reached states through closure measurements, substitution controls and an α \alpha sweep.

sections.heading: Knowledge Distillation for Language Models.
sections.text: Distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s output distribution Hinton et al. (2015) ; Rao et al. (2024) ; Jin et al. (2026) , extended to sequences generated by the teacher Kim and Rush (2016) and to other divergences Wen et al. (2023) ; Xu et al. (2024) survey the area. On-policy methods evaluate the loss on the student’s own samples Lin et al. (2020) ; Agarwal et al. (2024) ; Fu et al. (2026) ; Rao et al. (2026b) and now train production models Yang et al. (2025) ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) . DistiLLM Ko et al. (2024) ; Ko et al. (2025) mixes fixed and student-generated outputs under a skewed divergence, and TAID Shing et al. (2025) moves the training target from the student toward the teacher over training. These methods change the loss, its target, or the data mix Chen et al. (2026) ; Rao et al. (2026a) ; Rao et al. (2026c) ; CoRD keeps the on-policy loss and target and changes only where the states come from, so it applies unchanged to any per-state loss computed from both distributions.

sections.heading: Exposure Bias and Imitation Learning.
sections.text: Training on states the model would not visit at test time is the exposure-bias problem Bengio et al. (2015) ; Ranzato et al. (2016) . Scheduled sampling mixes reference and model tokens under a hand-set schedule Bengio et al. (2015) ; SEARN, DAgger and MiniLLM roll out a mixture of expert and learner Daumé III et al. (2009) ; Ross et al. (2011) ; Gu et al. (2024) , the last with importance weights. Their mixing follows a schedule or a fixed probability; in CoRD the probability of intervening at a token is the current disagreement itself, so no schedule is needed and interventions vanish as student and target agree. Section 5 includes a DAgger-style control with the same average rate.

sections.heading: Speculative Decoding and Interleaved Sampling.
sections.text: Speculative decoding lets a draft model propose tokens that a rejection sampler accepts or replaces so that the output follows the target exactly Leviathan et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2023) ; the sampler is a maximal coupling Lindvall (1992) . DistillSpec Zhou et al. (2024) uses distillation to improve the draft; CoRD conversely uses the sampler to improve distillation. Other recent work lets the teacher take over parts of the rollout when the student drifts Xu et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026b) , draws rollouts from a weaker negative policy Hwang et al. (2026) , or repairs the OPD objective itself Fu et al. (2026) ; none samples from an explicit target with an exact rejection rule. The closest prior work is SKD Xu et al. (2025) , where a student proposal outside the teacher’s top- K K tokens is replaced by a teacher sample. Its replacement can be any teacher token, including ones the student already overweights, and its acceptance set is fixed by K K , so its intervention rate is not tied to the distance between the two distributions. CoRD replaces only from the residual ( q α − p S ) + (q_{\alpha}-p_{\mathrm{S}})_{+} , emits tokens that follow q α q_{\alpha} exactly, intervenes at the rate TV ⁡ ( p S , q α ) \mathrm{TV}(p_{\mathrm{S}},q_{\alpha}) , and moves continuously from OPD ( α = 0 \alpha=0 ) to teacher-weighted states ( α = 1 \alpha=1 ). Section 4.3 compares the two under the same loss.

sections.heading: The Coupled Sampler.
sections.text: Algorithm 1 gives the rollout. The student proposes a ∼ p S a\sim p_{\mathrm{S}} , which is kept with probability min ⁡ ( 1 , q α ​ ( a ) / p S ​ ( a ) ) \min(1,q_{\alpha}(a)/p_{\mathrm{S}}(a)) . Otherwise a replacement is drawn from the normalized residual ( q α − p S ) + (q_{\alpha}-p_{\mathrm{S}})_{+} , the tokens that the target weights more heavily than the student does, and the rollout continues from the replacement. This is the rejection rule of speculative decoding Leviathan et al. (2023) , with the student as the draft and q α q_{\alpha} as the target. The rollout follows q α q_{\alpha} exactly: a draw from q α q_{\alpha} gives the same distribution of training states and the same expected update, and this shift of the states drives the gains. The coupling determines how the shift is realized. Among all ways to pair the student’s proposal with a draw from q α q_{\alpha} , it is the one that departs from the proposal least often, it makes every intervention explicit and measurable, and at α = 0 \alpha=0 it reproduces OPD bit for bit. Proposition 1 . Each emitted token is an exact sample from q α ( ⋅ ∣ s ) q_{\alpha}(\cdot\mid s) , and the probability of a replacement at state s s equals TV ( p S ( ⋅ ∣ s ) , q α ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ) \mathrm{TV}\big(p_{\mathrm{S}}(\cdot\mid s),q_{\alpha}(\cdot\mid s)\big) . The proof is the standard one for the rejection sampler of speculative decoding: a token v v is emitted with probability min ⁡ ( p S ​ ( v ) , q α ​ ( v ) ) + ( q α ​ ( v ) − p S ​ ( v ) ) + = q α ​ ( v ) \min(p_{\mathrm{S}}(v),q_{\alpha}(v))+(q_{\alpha}(v)-p_{\mathrm{S}}(v))_{+}=q_{\alpha}(v) , and the total rejection mass is ∑ v ( p S ​ ( v ) − q α ​ ( v ) ) + = TV ⁡ ( p S , q α ) \sum_{v}(p_{\mathrm{S}}(v)-q_{\alpha}(v))_{+}=\mathrm{TV}(p_{\mathrm{S}},q_{\alpha}) , the smallest probability with which any coupling of the two distributions can differ. Three consequences matter for distillation. The sampler intervenes only where the student and the target disagree, and in proportion to the disagreement, so the intervention rate is a measured quantity rather than a schedule and goes to zero as p S p_{\mathrm{S}} approaches p T p_{\mathrm{T}} . At α = 0 \alpha=0 the target equals the student, no proposal is ever rejected, and the rollout, the loss and the gradient are identical to OPD. And a replacement is sampled in proportion to the excess q α ​ ( v ) − p S ​ ( v ) q_{\alpha}(v)-p_{\mathrm{S}}(v) . On a three-token vocabulary with α = 0.6 \alpha=0.6 , student proposals are kept whenever possible and replaced only when necessary, so the emitted token follows q α q_{\alpha} exactly.

sections.heading: A Worked Example.
sections.text: In Figure 2 the student overweights a a and the teacher prefers c c , so the sampler rejects a proposal of a a with probability 0.41 and never rejects b b or c c . The replacement comes from the residual, which puts 82% of its mass on c c and none on a a : the rollout is pushed toward the token the student underweights, and only as often as needed, 24% of the time, to make the emitted token follow q α q_{\alpha} . A rule that replaces every token outside the teacher’s top-1 with a teacher sample, as SKD does with K = 1 K=1 , would intervene 90% of the time and could still emit a a .

sections.heading: Objective.
sections.text: The loss remains the full-vocabulary reverse KL defined in Eq. ( 1 ), evaluated at states s ∼ d q α s\sim d_{q_{\alpha}} . Because the divergence is zero only when the two distributions coincide, the minimizer at every visited state is still p S = p T p_{\mathrm{S}}=p_{\mathrm{T}} ; CoRD changes which states are weighted, not the per-state minimizer. During training the realized replacement rate tracks the mean total-variation distance computed from the same logits. As verified in Appendix B , the α = 0 \alpha=0 sampler reproduces the OPD gradient exactly.

sections.heading: No Importance Correction.
sections.text: Training on states from d q α d_{q_{\alpha}} rather than d p S d_{p_{\mathrm{S}}} is the point of the method, so we do not reweight the visited states back to the student’s distribution. Such a correction, a product of ratios p S / q α p_{\mathrm{S}}/q_{\alpha} along the prefix, would undo the shift and its variance would grow with the length of the rollout. As in OPD, the unchanged per-state loss is applied to the visited states, the sampling distribution is treated as fixed, and the gradient flows only through p S p_{\mathrm{S}} .

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We distill six base students from two model families: (i) Qwen3-0.6B-Base, Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base from Qwen3-8B-Base Yang et al. (2025) , (ii) Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, Qwen3.5-2B-Base and Qwen3.5-4B-Base from Qwen3.5-9B-Base Qwen Team (2026) . Students and teachers in a family share a tokenizer, which the coupling requires.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Unless noted, every run trains for 80 steps on 256 prompts per step, drawn in one fixed order from a fixed set of about 5,000 problems of the MATH training set Hendrycks et al. (2021) , with at most 320 new tokens per rollout, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} and the full-vocabulary reverse KL loss. Prompts use a fixed two-shot completion format. OPD and CoRD use the same code, data, data order and number of steps, and differ only in α \alpha : 0 for OPD and 0.6 for CoRD throughout. Section 5 shows how other values of α \alpha behave.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate students on MATH500 Hendrycks et al. (2021) ; Lightman et al. (2024) , AIME24 and AIME25 Mathematical Association of America (2024) ; Mathematical Association of America (2025) , AMC23 Mathematical Association of America (2023) and GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) , drawing 16 samples per problem at temperature 1.0 with a 4096-token limit in the training prompt format. Answers are scored by the SimpleRL-Zoo math checker Zeng et al. (2025) , and pass@ k k uses the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. (2021) . No hyperparameter or checkpoint was selected on these sets.

sections.heading: 4.1 Main Results
sections.text: Table 1 shows that CoRD improves average pass@1 and pass@8 over OPD for all six students. Average pass@1 rises by 0.9 to 2.0 percentage points and average pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points across the five benchmarks. Pass@16 is less uniform (Appendix Table 6 ): Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-4B gain 3.0 and 4.6 points on average, respectively, while Qwen3-1.7B is 0.1 points lower. Table 2 locates the largest within-student pass@16 gains: grouping all 1,919 problems by how many of 16 samples the untrained student solved, every student’s largest gain is on problems solved at most three times initially, reaching 5.9 points on never-solved problems for Qwen3.5-4B and 6.2 points on rarely solved ones for Qwen3-0.6B. sections.heading: 4.2 Learning Curves
sections.text: Figure 3 shows how the two samplers train. The reverse KL at the visited states, averaged over five steps, stays higher under CoRD for every student throughout the 80 steps: the coupled sampler keeps routing the rollouts through states where the student is still far from the teacher, so the loss at the visited states stays larger, whereas on OPD’s own states it quickly falls. On a held-out slice of the training distribution, CoRD ends above OPD for all six students.

sections.heading: 4.3 Comparison with SKD
sections.text: SKD Xu et al. (2025) also lets the teacher intervene in the student’s rollout. To compare the two sampling rules alone, we run SKD’s published rule, which replaces a proposal outside the teacher’s top 25 tokens by a teacher sample, with the same reverse KL loss, data, steps and per-step cost, for Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base and Qwen3.5-2B-Base; these are the rows “SKD” in Table 1 . SKD lands between OPD and CoRD on both averages for both students: it gains 0.6 and 0.2 points of average pass@1 over OPD, respectively, where CoRD gains 1.1 and 0.9 points. The two rules differ in how often, where and with what they intervene. With K = 25 K=25 , SKD replaces fewer than 1% of the tokens, 0.7% and 0.6% on average over training, because the student’s proposal almost always falls inside the teacher’s top 25 even where the two distributions differ substantially; CoRD replaces 6.8% and 5.7%, exactly the total-variation distance to its target. A top- K K rule asks whether the student’s token is plausible to the teacher, and where both models spread their mass over many reasonable continuations it accepts almost every proposal; the coupling moves exactly the excess of the target over the student, so supervision shifts toward the teacher wherever the two distributions differ, in proportion to how much they differ.

sections.heading: 4.4 OPD with Twice the Steps
sections.text: Because the coupled rollout queries the teacher during generation, we also give OPD twice the training steps: we train OPD on Qwen3.5-2B-Base for 160 steps, twice as many as CoRD . The extra steps do not help. The corresponding “OPD, 160 steps” row in Table 1 has average pass@1 of 15.1 and pass@8 of 35.6, below the 80-step OPD values of 16.0 and 35.7 and the 80-step CoRD values of 16.9 and 37.5.

sections.heading: 5 Learning in the Blind Spot
sections.text: We now ask where the gains come from. The analyses in this section distill the instruction-tuned Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B-Base, called 1.7B and 4B below, from Qwen3-8B-Base on MATH Hendrycks et al. (2021) for 40 steps, otherwise with the recipe of Section 4 .

sections.heading: CoRD Closes the Teacher-Side Gap.
sections.text: The first two rows of Table 3 show the effect of the sampler on the two sets. On teacher-reached states CoRD closes 44.4% of the gap at 1.7B against 37.4% for OPD, and 21.7% against 15.0% at 4B. It does so without giving up the student’s own states, where closure improves at 4B while OPD barely moves. Figure 4 follows the 4B student over 80 steps. The two curves on teacher-reached states separate within the first eight steps, and CoRD reaches after 16 steps a closure that OPD does not reach in 80. sections.heading: The Direction of the Replacement Matters.
sections.text: A natural objection is that any perturbation of the rollout would help by diversifying the training states. We test three alternatives. Two keep the acceptance test of CoRD and replace the residual draw by a uniform random token or by a token drawn from the student’s average token distribution. The third, in the spirit of DAgger, lets the teacher act at randomly chosen positions: at each position the teacher’s own sample replaces the student’s with a probability equal to CoRD ’s batch-mean replacement probability at that step, so the amount of intervention is comparable but its placement ignores where the two models disagree. At 1.7B all three intervene at least as often as CoRD in Table 3 , yet none comes close: the random and frequency rules fall below OPD on both students, and the DAgger-style mixing stays within two points of it. sections.text: The parameter α \alpha sets how far the target leans toward the teacher, and with it how often the sampler intervenes. Table 4 shows a clear trend: closure on teacher-reached states grows with α \alpha at both scales, and each tested α > 0 \alpha>0 closes more of the teacher-side gap than OPD. sections.heading: What the Student Gets Right.
sections.text: Accuracy can rise because the student formats answers more reliably or because the answers it commits to are more often correct. On the public benchmarks almost every sample ends in an extractable answer, 99.5 to 99.9% for every run of Table 1 , so the pass@1 gains of Table 1 are gains in the correctness of the student’s answers, not in their form.

sections.heading: Interventions Recede With Training.
sections.text: Because the replacement probability equals the current total-variation distance, the sampler withdraws as the student approaches the target. Figure 4 shows that in the 80-step run at 4B, the replacement rate falls from 6.9% at the first step to 4.9% at step 80, without any schedule.

sections.heading: The Effect Holds Across Teachers.
sections.text: With Qwen3-14B as the teacher of the 1.7B student for 20 steps, CoRD again closes more of the teacher-side gap than OPD, by 4.2 points, so the gain carries over to a second, larger teacher.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: On-policy distillation supervises the student only where the student already goes. CoRD widens that set by sampling each rollout from the maximal coupling of the student and a teacher-leaning target: the student’s token is kept where the two agree, and a token from the residual is substituted where they do not, exactly as often as they disagree. The loss, the data and the number of training steps stay as they are, and the method adds a single parameter: α = 0 \alpha=0 is OPD exactly, and one value, α = 0.6 \alpha=0.6 , serves all six students. The interventions need no schedule, because the replacement rate falls by itself as the student approaches the target. Across six base students from two model families on public benchmarks, this change improves average pass@1 and pass@8 for all six students. Pass@16 gains are more variable, but each student’s largest difficulty-bin gain occurs on problems it rarely or never solved before training. Frozen sets of teacher-reached states show that CoRD closes more of the gap on exactly the states the teacher reaches. Because the sampler needs only the teacher’s logits during generation, it combines with any change to the loss or its target.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: CoRD needs the teacher’s logits during the rollout. Our public-benchmark experiments cover base students up to 4B parameters and teachers up to 9B (14B in one analysis), all on mathematical reasoning; larger models and other tasks are untested. Student and teacher must share a tokenizer. The AIME sets each contain only 30 problems, so small differences in pass rates should be interpreted cautiously.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This work studies model distillation using public mathematical data and benchmarks; it involves no human subjects or personal data. Improving a student’s ability to follow a stronger model can also transfer that model’s errors, biases, or unsafe behavior, and the resulting capabilities may be used outside the evaluated setting. Our experiments therefore should not be interpreted as a safety evaluation or as evidence that distilled models are reliable in high-stakes applications. We encourage evaluation for the intended deployment context, including independent accuracy and safety checks, before use.

sections.heading: Appendix B Exactness of the Sampler
sections.text: Before any training we checked the implementation against the closed form. On small vocabularies, the histogram of emitted tokens agrees with q α q_{\alpha} for α ∈ { 0 , 0.3 , 0.6 , 1 } \alpha\in\{0,0.3,0.6,1\} , and the realized rejection rate agrees with the analytic total-variation distance to within 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} ; a sampler that replaces rejected tokens uniformly fails the same check by a wide margin. With the real 4B student and 8B teacher (200 prompts, 256 new tokens), the rejection rate agrees with the mean total-variation distance at every α \alpha , the α = 0 \alpha=0 sampler never rejects, and its gradient equals that of plain OPD exactly. During training of the 4B student ( α = 0.6 \alpha=0.6 , 40 steps), the realized replacement rate stays within 0.003 of the mean total-variation distance computed from the same logits at every step. Email: {xiaojun.meng,yuanpeng126,weijiansheng}@huawei.com Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, China Affiliation: Huawei Large Model Data Technology Lab Email: rao7jun@gmail.com Email: xieye-xin@qq.com Email: liuxuebo@hit.edu.cn Abstract On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student’s token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD . 1 Introduction The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has been driven by complementary progress in model architectures ( He et al., 2016 ; Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Yu et al., 2026a ) , data scale and quality ( Yuan et al., 2023 ; Rao et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026b ) , and training paradigms ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . Current research frontiers span theoretical explorations of learning dynamics and generalization ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) , generation across various modalities ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2026 ) , tool-augmented reasoning ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and interdisciplinary applications ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . Within this broad landscape, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a central paradigm for exploring complex reasoning and knowledge transfer. A key challenge is how to enable smaller student models to efficiently inherit the capabilities of stronger teachers. Figure 1: Overview of CoRD . (i) Left (OPD’s blind spot): On-policy distillation trains only on student rollouts. Teacher-preferred reasoning paths that the student rarely or never visits therefore receive little or no supervision. (ii) Right (our coupled sampler): CoRD keeps the same training loss and budget, but changes the rollout sampler. By coupling the student with a teacher-leaning target q α q_{\alpha} , it preserves agreeing tokens and replaces disagreements with underweighted target tokens. This maximal coupling steers rollouts into teacher-preferred states missed by OPD with the minimum possible intervention rate, minimally perturbing the student’s original trajectory. Among knowledge distillation methods, on-policy distillation (OPD) has become a commonly used approach to this challenge Agarwal et al. (2024) ; Gu et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2024) . The student generates its own rollouts and is trained to match the teacher’s full next-token distribution at every state it visits, usually by minimizing the reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence. Training on self-generated text removes the mismatch between teacher-forced training and free-running generation Bengio et al. (2015) ; Ranzato et al. (2016) ; Ross et al. (2011) , and the teacher’s dense, token-level signal replaces the single final reward of reinforcement learning. The same design also fixes where the supervision lands. Because states are drawn from the student, the teacher only ever comments on states the student already reaches. States the teacher would enter, such as the first step of a solution path the student considers unlikely, are sampled only as often as the student itself picks them, and corrected only that often. We measure this blind spot on frozen sets of states. Before training, the student is 1.5 to 2.4 times further from the teacher on states reached by the teacher’s distribution than on states it reaches itself, across the four students analyzed in Section 5 . On-policy training closes this gap only slowly: after 40 steps at 4B, OPD has removed 15.0% of the divergence on teacher-reached states, where the sampler we introduce removes 21.7%. Reaching those states requires steering the rollout toward the teacher while leaving it the student’s own text wherever the two agree. Speculative decoding already contains the right tool Leviathan et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2023) . Its rejection sampler, usually seen as an accelerator, realizes the maximal coupling of two token distributions Lindvall (1992) : a draft token is kept where the distributions agree and replaced by a draw from their difference where they do not. When used instead as a training sampler, this rule intervenes only where the student and the target disagree, and exactly as often as they disagree. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), illustrated in Figure 1 , which changes the rollout sampler of OPD and nothing else. At each position the student proposes a token, and the coupling with a tempered target q α ∝ p S 1 − α ​ p T α q_{\alpha}\propto p_{\mathrm{S}}^{1-\alpha}p_{\mathrm{T}}^{\alpha} either keeps it or substitutes a token from the residual mass that the student underweights. Every emitted token is an exact draw from q α q_{\alpha} , the probability of an intervention equals the total-variation distance between p S p_{\mathrm{S}} and q α q_{\alpha} , and α = 0 \alpha=0 recovers OPD bit for bit. The loss, the teacher, and the number of training steps stay as they are; only the distribution of training states moves toward the teacher. That shift is the source of the gain. The coupling is how CoRD reaches the shifted states while rewriting as little of the student’s own text as any exact sampler of q α q_{\alpha} can, and it splits every draw into an acceptance decision and a replacement direction, which Section 5 tests separately. The shift pays off on public benchmarks. Across six base students from two model families, CoRD improves average pass@1 and pass@8 over OPD on MATH500, AIME24, AIME25, AMC23 and GSM8K for every student in Table 1 ; on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, SKD’s published replacement rule Xu et al. (2025) , with the same loss and budget, lands between OPD and CoRD , and OPD trained for twice as many steps does not catch up. The difficulty breakdown shows that each student’s largest pass@16 gain is on problems it rarely or never solved before training, although the aggregate pass@16 gain is not positive for every student. Substitution rules that intervene at least as often but draw the replacement from elsewhere, namely a uniform token, a token from the student’s average distribution, or a teacher sample at randomly chosen positions, stay at or near OPD and far below CoRD , which ties the gain to where the rollouts are steered rather than to the act of intervening. Our contributions are as follows: • We measure the blind spot of on-policy distillation on frozen sets of teacher-reached states, where the student starts 1.5 to 2.4 times further from the teacher than on its own states, and show that OPD leaves most of it in place. • We propose CoRD , which trains on rollouts from a teacher-leaning target and realizes them with the speculative-decoding rejection sampler: exact draws from the target with the fewest possible replacements (the total-variation distance), and OPD as the special case α = 0 \alpha=0 . • We show gains in average pass@1 and pass@8 over OPD for all six base students on five public math benchmarks, and study teacher-reached states through closure measurements, substitution controls and an α \alpha sweep. 2 Related Work Knowledge Distillation for Language Models. Distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s output distribution Hinton et al. (2015) ; Rao et al. (2024) ; Jin et al. (2026) , extended to sequences generated by the teacher Kim and Rush (2016) and to other divergences Wen et al. (2023) ; Xu et al. (2024) survey the area. On-policy methods evaluate the loss on the student’s own samples Lin et al. (2020) ; Agarwal et al. (2024) ; Fu et al. (2026) ; Rao et al. (2026b) and now train production models Yang et al. (2025) ; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab (2025) . DistiLLM Ko et al. (2024) ; Ko et al. (2025) mixes fixed and student-generated outputs under a skewed divergence, and TAID Shing et al. (2025) moves the training target from the student toward the teacher over training. These methods change the loss, its target, or the data mix Chen et al. (2026) ; Rao et al. (2026a) ; Rao et al. (2026c) ; CoRD keeps the on-policy loss and target and changes only where the states come from, so it applies unchanged to any per-state loss computed from both distributions. Exposure Bias and Imitation Learning. Training on states the model would not visit at test time is the exposure-bias problem Bengio et al. (2015) ; Ranzato et al. (2016) . Scheduled sampling mixes reference and model tokens under a hand-set schedule Bengio et al. (2015) ; SEARN, DAgger and MiniLLM roll out a mixture of expert and learner Daumé III et al. (2009) ; Ross et al. (2011) ; Gu et al. (2024) , the last with importance weights. Their mixing follows a schedule or a fixed probability; in CoRD the probability of intervening at a token is the current disagreement itself, so no schedule is needed and interventions vanish as student and target agree. Section 5 includes a DAgger-style control with the same average rate. Speculative Decoding and Interleaved Sampling. Speculative decoding lets a draft model propose tokens that a rejection sampler accepts or replaces so that the output follows the target exactly Leviathan et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2023) ; the sampler is a maximal coupling Lindvall (1992) . DistillSpec Zhou et al. (2024) uses distillation to improve the draft; CoRD conversely uses the sampler to improve distillation. Other recent work lets the teacher take over parts of the rollout when the student drifts Xu et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026b) , draws rollouts from a weaker negative policy Hwang et al. (2026) , or repairs the OPD objective itself Fu et al. (2026) ; none samples from an explicit target with an exact rejection rule. The closest prior work is SKD Xu et al. (2025) , where a student proposal outside the teacher’s top- K K tokens is replaced by a teacher sample. Its replacement can be any teacher token, including ones the student already overweights, and its acceptance set is fixed by K K , so its intervention rate is not tied to the distance between the two distributions. CoRD replaces only from the residual ( q α − p S ) + (q_{\alpha}-p_{\mathrm{S}})_{+} , emits tokens that follow q α q_{\alpha} exactly, intervenes at the rate TV ⁡ ( p S , q α ) \mathrm{TV}(p_{\mathrm{S}},q_{\alpha}) , and moves continuously from OPD ( α = 0 \alpha=0 ) to teacher-weighted states ( α = 1 \alpha=1 ). Section 4.3 compares the two under the same loss. 3 Method On-Policy Distillation. A student policy p S ( ⋅ ∣ s ) p_{\mathrm{S}}(\cdot\mid s) is trained toward a frozen teacher p T ( ⋅ ∣ s ) p_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid s) , where a state s s is a prompt followed by a partial response. OPD minimizes the reverse KL divergence at the states visited by the student’s own rollouts, ℒ OPD = 𝔼 s ∼ d p S [ D KL ( p S ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ∥ p T ( ⋅ ∣ s ) ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{OPD}}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{p_{\mathrm{S}}}}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{\mathrm{S}}(\cdot\mid s)\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid s)\big)\big], (1) where d p S d_{p_{\mathrm{S}}} is the distribution of states induced by sampling from p S p_{\mathrm{S}} and the divergence is computed over the full vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . The loss supervises every visited state densely, but the visited states come from d p S d_{p_{\mathrm{S}}} alone. A Teacher-Leaning Target. CoRD widens that set by sampling each rollout from the maximal coupling of the student and a teacher-leaning target: the student’s token is kept where the two agree, and a token from the residual is substituted where they do not, exactly as often as they disagree. The loss, the data and the number of training steps stay as they are, and the method adds a single parameter: α = 0 \alpha=0 is OPD exactly, and one value, α = 0.6 \alpha=0.6 , serves all six students. The interventions need no schedule, because the replacement rate falls by itself as the student approaches the target. Across six base students from two model families on public benchmarks, this change improves average pass@1 and pass@8 for all six students. Pass@16 gains are more variable, but each student’s largest difficulty-bin gain occurs on problems it rarely or never solved before training. Frozen sets of teacher-reached states show that CoRD closes more of the gap on exactly the states the teacher reaches. Because the sampler needs only the teacher’s logits during generation, it combines with any change to the loss or its target. Limitations CoRD needs the teacher’s logits during the rollout. Our public-benchmark experiments cover base students up to 4B parameters and teachers up to 9B (14B in one analysis), all on mathematical reasoning; larger models and other tasks are untested. Student and teacher must share a tokenizer. The AIME sets each contain only 30 problems, so small differences in pass rates should be interpreted cautiously. Ethical Considerations This work studies model distillation using public mathematical data and benchmarks; it involves no human subjects or personal data. Improving a student’s ability to follow a stronger model can also transfer that model’s errors, biases, or unsafe behavior, and the resulting capabilities may be used outside the evaluated setting. Our experiments therefore should not be interpreted as a safety evaluation or as evidence that distilled models are reliable in high-stakes applications. We encourage evaluation for the intended deployment context, including independent accuracy and safety checks, before use. References Agarwal et al.
